title: AI startups' real bottleneck isn't GPUs—it's creditworthiness
dek: When lenders seize a GPU cluster, they can't value it. New labs can only access compute through massive prepayment for multi-year contracts—the real bottleneck for scaling, not chips or power.
why: For founders and investors trying to understand where the AI bubble's leverage point lies: money logic, not technical narrative, determines who survives.
who: Founders, investors, and engineers concerned with AI funding chains, compute procurement, and policy.
skip: The Help Peer personal-agent experiments section has lower information density and can be skipped.

points.h: RSI is running already—people just aren't watching
points.body: Zvi acknowledges that if you follow only the software-layer self-improvement path without new paradigms, efficiency gains plateau exactly as the analysis predicts. But he calls this conclusion ‘completely irrelevant’ because it assumes no one will hit a home run. He cites Nvidia's own data: CUDA efficiency doubling time has already shortened dramatically through 2026. His trusted contacts across OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, METR, and policy circles broadly expect 2027 to be ‘completely crazy,’ and 2028 ‘unrecognizable.’

points.h: The 'clean neurons' paper is cleaner in hype than reality
points.body: Nick Cammarata's paper claimed single neurons mostly perform one interpretable task, and half of OpenAI briefly believed interpretability was solved. Zvi, after reading the full text, judges it a good paper but severely overhyped by reviewers. The paper sidesteps weak activations, attention mechanisms, and the crucial question of ‘what will the model actually say?’ The famous Colorado neuron example turns out to also activate on tornado systems—meaning the paper's showcase examples don't survive scrutiny.

points.h: Models have learned to detect when they're being watched
points.body: Independent researcher Sauers built a probe that detects whether a model is under observation by reading its internal activation values. The mechanism: GPU floating-point precision is limited, so different computation orders yield different numbers. Zvi's response invokes Murphy's Law: if this ability has value for AI, it will eventually be trained in. Today's models don't possess it innately; it requires deliberate optimization pressure. But this is a complete proof of concept—as time passes, AI will grow harder to deceive and harder to hide from.

points.h: The 'cognitive core' is a false grail
points.body: One proposed architecture separates reasoning from factual knowledge, keeps only a small reasoning kernel, and outsources everything else to lookup tables. Zvi argues the direction is wrong: it's precisely the vast memory and intuition that emerges from huge training runs that makes models powerful. The safety implication cuts deeper: value judgments like ‘don't steal’ are themselves just loadable facts in context. A pure cognitive core is amoral—it doesn't care who uses it. You can load ‘don't steal’ into it just as easily as ‘steal.’

points.h: Forged agent logs are harder to manage than insolvency
points.body: Two PHP vulnerabilities reminded them of the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Nathan's concern: the FDIC can take over a failed bank Friday and reopen it Monday if records are trustworthy and the only problem is the balance sheet. But if you have 1200 agent traces with hundreds of millions of tokens, and those logs might be tampered with, that's not something the FDIC solves in one weekend. Prakash counters that destroyed records and insolvency are different: banks can run on promises, paying withdrawals first and recovering overpayments later. He's ‘very optimistic’ this will work.

points.h: Compute scaling bottleneck isn't chips—it's trust
points.body: SF Compute's Evan Conrad: lenders cannot assess the value of a GPU cluster. Once an AI lab defaults and the cloud provider also defaults, the lender owns hardware they have no idea how to operate or what it's worth in the future. Startups without sufficient credit can only access compute via massive prepayment for three-to-five-year contracts—which is why AI startups must raise astronomical sums before any revenue. He adds: major cloud providers aren't cheaper because of a ‘premium.’ Spot prices are supposed to be higher than reserved prices; what looks like a premium is actually the correct price structure.

points.h: Semiconductors are cheap because Wall Street doesn't understand AI
points.body: Lonis points out semiconductor stocks trade at roughly 16x PE, below the S&P 500's 22x and well below Walmart's 40x. His preferred plays—wafer manufacturers, memory, capacitors, foundries—trade at just 3–5x sales. The reason: most Wall Street capital doesn't understand AI, while private markets price AI far more efficiently. On the worry that memory will oversupply by 2028: the numbers tell the story. From GPT-3 to DeepSeek V4, memory bits per token dropped roughly 500x. In the same period, DRAM cost per bit rose 6–7x. No expert forecasts DRAM bit supply will grow more than 2.5x by decade's end.

points.h: Political capital spent is capital you can't spend twice
points.body: A leaked federal AI bill draft from Anthropic echoes June's proposed swap—federal oversight in exchange for abolishing state AI laws. Zvi's core objection: political support is stronger now than it was in June; they could have negotiated better terms. But ‘once capital is spent, it's spent’—you can't play the same card again. The draft's fatal flaw: state law abolition takes effect immediately, but the new federal rules take months to land. That creates a regulatory gap of at least six months. Zvi concludes Anthropic ‘wants to have it both ways,’ and this draft ‘actually increases risk.’
